I used to MUD a VERY long time ago when GMud32 and ANSI support were still separately bundled... Naturally I'm well out the loop now that I'm returning.

What are some of the better MUD clients/what do most of you use and why? I've checked out the Wikipedia article comparing various clients but I'm more interested in the feel of the client without diving into this massive list.

I'm using TinTin++. It's a terminal client, and uses the tt++ scripting language. I use it 'cause of it's automapper feature, which is very useful, but it easily gets messed up. Features of the program (which I copied from the webpage):

TinTin++ supports MCCP (Mud Client Compression Protocol), MMCP (Mud Master Chat Protocol), xterm 256 colors, most TELNET options used by MUDs, as well as those required to login via telnet on Linux / Mac OS X servers, and an auto mapper with a VT100 map display. Being a console client TinTin++ works with most screen readers, and its non graphical command interface makes the client particularly screen reader / blind friendly.

Program features are support for regular expression enabled triggers, aliases, gags, highlights, substitutions, macros, timers, delayed responses, events, associative arrays, text formatting, searching the scrollback buffer, 64 bit floating point logical and arithmatic expressions, an auto mapper with a VT100 map display, multiple sessions, loading and parsing of files, execution of command line scripts, running command line programs within the client (such as ssh and sftp) with full scripting capabilities, splitscreen to separate client input and mud output, drawing of VT100 status bars, and tab completion on the scrollback buffer.

If you prefer GUIs, go with MUSHClient on windows and Mudlet on anything else.

OK, suppose I have a kid just like you, named Timmy. Timmy is always leaving his dirty shirts all over the house, just like you do. So I pick them up, wash them, and put them in a big huge drawer. When Timmy says "daddy I need a shirt" I just go to the shirt drawer and pull out a shirt.

The problem is, Timmy is growing up, just like you. He's always getting bigger, so some of the old shirts just don't fit him anymore. So when Timmy goes up a size, say to a Boys Size 8, I don't know it until he tells me "Daddy this shirt's too small!". So I look at the shirt, and if I see like it's a Size 7, then I know he can't wear Size 7 anymore, so then I go through the entire shirt drawer, looking at the label on every shirt, and I put all the ones that are Size 7 or smaller and put them in a big box for the little neighborhood kids who have no nice shirts to wear. I call these "explicitly deleted shirts".

But the drawer is so big, and Timmy has so many thousands of shirts, it takes me days and days to go through them all when he goes up a size, so I thought of a really smart way to do it: now, when Timmy needs a shirt, I just grab a shirt out of the drawer and look at the size: if it's smaller than his current size, I call it an "implicitly invalidated shirt", and I throw it in the little neighborhood kid's box, and then just pull out another shirt, again and again until there's one he can wear.

This way, the little neighborhood kids still get shirts, but like one a week, instead of getting like fifty all of a sudden once a year. Everyone is happy!
